title: What Are the "Look Fors" in Secondary Literacy Programs?
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: Responding to a district that is weighing a textbook adoption while some teachers want to teach only novels, Timothy Shanahan distils the "look fors" of a sound middle and high school ELA program from the Carnegie Corporation, Common Core, College Board and other authoritative sources. His central claim is that novel study alone cannot meet the learning requirements these sources set out, though novels still deserve a place. He lists explicit reading and writing instruction, a wide range of texts, cultural inclusion, sufficiently demanding texts, direct teaching of vocabulary, morphology, syntax and text structure, motivational support, disciplinary literacy and a clear overall structure. He is candid about where he differs from colleagues, noting that evidence is thin that readers learn more from authors who share their background, while still endorsing diverse reading. He also points out that popular high school novels often fall below the text complexity the state standards require.
points: Shanahan argues that a program built only on novels would leave out the analytical writing from sources that every set of standards requires.
Because reading comprehension is not a skill in itself, the texts students read matter as much as the teaching: they supply genre knowledge, world knowledge and language demands.

Many beloved high school novels, such as Of Mice and Men or The Outsiders, place minimal linguistic demands on students, so text complexity must be checked against the Lexile levels the state requires.
Teens are biologically driven toward autonomy, so a good program offers choice and compelling reasons for participating rather than simply telling them what to learn.
A clear horizontal and vertical structure, with review and repetition across units and years, is presented as wise stewardship compared with each teacher selecting novels independently.
quotes: Reading comprehension is not a skill per se. Proficient comprehension depends upon understanding how different texts work, knowledge of the world, competence with language, and so on.

In my experience, in classes focused solely or mainly on novel reading, writing is allotted a minor role. If there’s one thing all these sources agree on, it’s that analytical writing should be allotted substantial attention in the ELA curriculum.

The extent of such requirements reveals why novel reading alone would be insufficient. It would be impossible for kids to get multiple opportunities to take on that range of texts, if their instructional reading was limited to novels.

My uncertainty as to potency of such literature in terms of improving reading achievement should not be interpreted as an opposition to including texts that reflect a wide range of cultural diversity. Nothing could be further from the truth.

English teachers have become quite adept at identifying worthwhile texts (in terms of literary merit, cultural value, thematic relevance, etc.) that are relatively easy for their students to read. Books like Of Mice and Men, The Outsiders, Lord of the Flies, Catcher in the Rye, To Kill a Mockingbird, Fahrenheit 451, no matter their literary value, place minimal linguistic demands on students.

Teens are not like younger children. They’re biologically programmed to strive for autonomy and independence (e.g., Branje, de Moor, Spitzer, & Becht, 2021). Telling them what to do – what to learn – tends to have limited effectiveness.

When each teacher selects novels and determines the instruction to go with them, there tends to be a lot of overlap and repetition, and some important issues may be missed. Requiring that the ELA program have comprehensiveness, continuity, and sufficient review and repetition is wise stewardship.
